summary: A status report on the network numbers and autonomous system numbers used in the Internet. As of 1 March 1987, the Network Information Center at SRI International took over assigning them, and this RFC records the assignments at the time of transfer. It was replaced by RFC 1020 and RFC 1117.

eli5.summary: It is a list of who owns which network addresses, written down on the day a new office started handing them out.

questions: who assigned internet network numbers in 1987
what is an ip network number
what are the ip address classes
how is a class b network different from a class c network
subtitle: A status report of Internet network numbers and autonomous system assignments as of March 1987.

tldr.problem: The Internet grows as new networks join, and each needs a unique network number. The assignment of these numbers must be tracked and distributed to all participating organizations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 997 is a snapshot of all assigned Internet network numbers and autonomous system numbers as of March 1987, organized by IP address class (A, B, C, D, E) and showing the organization, location, and responsible contact for each assignment.
tldr.outcome: This RFC transferred administrative responsibility for network number assignment from the original RFC authors to the Network Information Center at SRI International. Future editions would update periodically. RFC 997 was replaced by RFC 1020 and RFC 1117.

today: RFC 997 has been obsoleted by RFC 1020 and RFC 1117. The administrative approach of publishing a periodic RFC with all assignments was eventually replaced by online databases and automated systems as the Internet exploded in size. Today, the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) and regional registries maintain and publish address allocations. However, the fundamental structure of IP addressing classes and the principle of centralized assignment that RFC 997 documented remain part of Internet architecture, though Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) has largely replaced the strict class boundaries.

sections.title: Internet Address Classes and Assignment
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol divides the 32-bit address space into five classes. Class A has a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address, allowing 128 networks (high-order bit is 0). Class B has a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address, allowing 16,384 networks (high-order bits are 10). Class C has a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address, allowing 2,097,152 networks (high-order bits are 110). Class D addresses are reserved for multicast (high-order bits are 1110), and Class E addresses are reserved for future use (high-order bits are 1111).

Network numbers are assigned by the Network Information Center, with a one-character prefix indicating the user category: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-defense), and C for Commercial. Independent networks that use IP but are not connected to the Internet are marked with an asterisk. Temporary addresses during transitions are marked with a T suffix.
sections.eli5: The 32-bit address is divided into a network part and a host part. Depending on how you divide it, you get Class A (big networks, few of them), Class B (medium networks), or Class C (small networks, many of them). Each organization that joins the Internet gets a network number from the phone book.

sections.title: Special Addresses and Notation
sections.content:
Some addresses have special meanings. The address zero (for example, 0.0.0.37) means 'this host on this network'. The address of all ones (for example, 128.9.255.255) means 'all hosts on this network'. Class A network 127 is reserved for loopback, meaning packets sent to any address in 127.x.x.x loop back inside the sending host and never leave the network.

The RFC uses dotted-decimal notation to write addresses: four decimal numbers separated by periods, such as 10.1.0.52 for the address 010.001.000.052. This notation is easier to read and write than binary or hexadecimal. In the listings below, class A networks use the pattern nnn.rrr.rrr.rrr (where n is network, r is local address), class B uses nnn.nnn.rrr.rrr, and class C uses nnn.nnn.nnn.rrr.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are reserved for special purposes, like 127 for talking to yourself, and 255 for talking to everyone. Addresses are written as four numbers separated by dots to make them easier to read: 192.168.1.1 instead of binary.

sections.title: Class A Network Assignments
sections.content:
This section lists every Class A network number assigned as of March 1, 1987. Notable assignments include 10.rrr.rrr.rrr for ARPANET, 26.rrr.rrr.rrr for MILNET, and 127.rrr.rrr.rrr for loopback. The list shows that most Class A networks are assigned to large research institutions, defense projects, and corporations. Many entries carry a contact name and reference number (such as [4,SA2]) pointing to the responsible person in the NIC database.

The list includes temporary assignments (marked with T) that were being transitioned to permanent numbers, and reserved or unassigned ranges. The entries give a snapshot of the Internet at a moment when it was still small enough to list every assigned number; this would become impossible as the Internet grew.
sections.eli5: Here are all the Class A networks: who owns them, where they are, and whom to call if you need to know more. Class A networks are like area codes in the phone system—there are only 128 of them, and each covers a huge area.

sections.title: Class B and C Networks
sections.content:
The RFC also lists assigned Class B networks (14-bit network number) and Class C networks (21-bit network number). Class B assignments include networks at major universities (Yale, MIT, Stanford), corporations (HP, DEC, Xerox), and government research facilities. Class C networks, being much more numerous, are not exhaustively listed in detail; instead, the RFC groups related assignments together (for example, all of the Penn State subnets, all of the Bragg networks).

Each listing includes the network number in dotted-decimal notation, the network name (such as YALE-NET or MIT-NET), a brief description of what the network is, and references. Some networks are marked as research (R), defense (D), government (G), or commercial (C), and some are marked with an asterisk to indicate they are independent networks not directly connected to the Internet.
sections.eli5: Class B networks belong to medium-sized organizations like universities and research centers. Class C networks are for smaller organizations. The RFC lists thousands of them to show everyone who is on the Internet and what their numbers are.

sections.title: Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content:
In addition to network numbers, the RFC documents Autonomous System numbers (AS numbers), which identify groups of networks under a single administrative authority. An autonomous system runs its own routing protocols internally (an Interior Gateway Protocol) and exchanges routing information with other autonomous systems using an Exterior Gateway Protocol.

The RFC notes that AS numbers are assigned similarly to network numbers, with administrative categories and contact information. The system allows a large organization or region to manage its own networks while still participating in the global Internet. As routing protocols matured, AS numbers became essential for coordinating routing between large organizations.
sections.eli5: A network number says 'here is one connection to the Internet'. An autonomous system number says 'here is a whole group of networks that one organization runs, and they have their own internal post office'.

sections.title: Responsibility and Maintenance
sections.content:
The RFC is dated March 1987 and marks the moment when administrative responsibility for network number assignment transferred from the original RFC authors (Jon Postel and others at ISI) to the newly established Network Information Center at SRI International. The NIC Hostmaster (reachable at HOSTMASTER@SRI-NIC.ARPA or by phone) became the official point of contact for network number assignments.

The RFC states it 'will be updated periodically', acknowledging that assignments will continue. The format and structure set by this RFC (listing organizations, categories, responsible contacts, and references) established the template for all future RFC-based network registries. Future versions would continue to document assignments in the same format until the Internet grew too large for simple listings.
sections.eli5: This RFC was the day the job of handing out network numbers moved from the creators of the Internet to a help desk. They promised to keep the list up to date as the Internet grew.
